---
title: "2.1 — Clauses, CNF, and conversion"
---

> **Where you are.** Course 1 built a *human-style* prover (natural deduction). Course 2 builds a
> *machine-style* one: **resolution**, the engine behind SAT and SMT. Resolution doesn't work on arbitrary
> formulas — it works on **clauses**. This slice sets up clauses, their semantics, and a conversion from
> `Form`, then proves the conversion faithful and derives the bridge that makes resolution a *proof*
> method: **a formula is valid exactly when the clauses of its negation are unsatisfiable.** Code
> graduates into `Principia.Resolution.Cnf`.

## 1. The question

Resolution is *refutation-based*: instead of proving `φ` directly, it assumes `∼φ` and derives a
contradiction. To do that mechanically it needs a uniform shape — **conjunctive normal form**: an AND of
ORs of literals. So two things are needed: (a) a data type for clause sets with a notion of
(un)satisfiability, and (b) a conversion `Form → Cnf` that *preserves meaning*, so refuting the converted
negation really does prove the original.

## 2. Clauses and CNF

```lean
structure Lit where               -- a literal: a variable with a polarity
  var : Nat
  pol : Bool                       -- true = positive (var), false = negative (¬var)
abbrev Clause := List Lit          -- a clause is a DISJUNCTION of literals
abbrev Cnf := List Clause          -- a CNF is a CONJUNCTION of clauses
```

The semantics read off the structure: a literal is true per its polarity; a clause is true if *some*
literal is; a clause set is true if *every* clause is.

```lean
def Lit.eval    v l := if l.pol then v l.var else !(v l.var)
def Clause.eval v c := c.any (Lit.eval v)     -- ∨ over the literals
def Cnf.eval    v s := s.all (Clause.eval v)   -- ∧ over the clauses
```

Two boundary cases matter. The **empty clause `[]`** has no literal to satisfy, so `Clause.eval v [] =
false` — it is **`□`, the unsatisfiable clause**. The **empty clause set `[]`** is a conjunction of nothing,
so `Cnf.eval v [] = true` — trivially satisfiable. A clause set is `Unsat` when *no* valuation satisfies
it: `∀ v, Cnf.eval v s = false`. Deriving `□` will be how resolution witnesses unsatisfiability.

## 3. Converting a formula to CNF

The classic conversion pushes negations inward (to literals) and distributes `∨` over `∧`. We do both at
once with a **polarity flag** `b`: `toCnf b φ` is a clause set for `φ` if `b = true`, for `∼φ` if `b =
false`. Carrying `b` down means `¬` never appears as a connective — it only flips a literal's polarity.

```lean
def toCnf : Bool → Form → Cnf
  | b, .var n   => [[{var := n, pol := b}]]              -- a single literal, polarity = b
  | b, .fls     => if b then [[]] else []                 -- ⊥ → □ (false);  ¬⊥ = ⊤ → [] (true)
  | b, .and a c => if b then toCnf true a ++ toCnf true c  -- a∧c: append the clause sets
                        else distribute (toCnf false a) (toCnf false c)   -- ¬(a∧c) = ¬a ∨ ¬c
  | b, .or a c  => if b then distribute (toCnf true a) (toCnf true c)      -- a∨c: distribute
                        else toCnf false a ++ toCnf false c                 -- ¬(a∨c) = ¬a ∧ ¬c
  | b, .imp a c => if b then distribute (toCnf false a) (toCnf true c)     -- a⇒c = ¬a ∨ c
                        else toCnf true a ++ toCnf false c                  -- ¬(a⇒c) = a ∧ ¬c
```

`distribute s1 s2` is the CNF of `s1 ∨ s2`: pair every clause of `s1` with every clause of `s2` and
concatenate (`s1.flatMap (fun c1 => s2.map (c1 ++ ·))`). The key fact (given to you as `distribute_eval`)
is that this computes the disjunction: `Cnf.eval v (distribute s1 s2) = Cnf.eval v s1 || Cnf.eval v s2` —
the only subtle Boolean step is `(A∨C) ∧ (B∨C) = (A∧B)∨C`.

**Correctness** (`toCnf_eval`, your first goal): `Cnf.eval v (toCnf b φ)` equals `eval v φ` when `b =
true`, and `!eval v φ` when `b = false`. By induction on `φ`, generalizing `b`; each connective splits on
`b` and rebuilds with `distribute_eval` / `cnf_eval_append` and the induction hypotheses, finishing with a
Boolean truth-table check (the De Morgan dualities).

## 4. The bridge: refutation proves validity

Now the payoff (`taut_iff_cnf_unsat`, your second goal):

```lean
Form.Tautology φ ↔ (toCnf false φ).Unsat
```

Read it: **`φ` is valid ⟺ the clauses of `∼φ` are unsatisfiable.** It's immediate from `toCnf_eval` at
`b = false`: `Cnf.eval v (toCnf false φ) = !eval v φ`, which is `false` for *all* `v` exactly when `eval v
φ = true` for all `v` — i.e. `φ` is a tautology. This is why a *refutation* engine is a *proof* engine: to
establish `φ`, convert `∼φ` to clauses and show they can't all be satisfied. Course 1 connects too — by
`provable_iff_tautology`, `⊢ φ` iff `φ` is valid iff `toCnf false φ` is unsatisfiable, so the
natural-deduction and resolution provers decide the very same problem.

## 5. Prove it

The structures, plumbing, `distribute_eval`, and `toCnf` are given. Prove
(`make lab C=02-resolution/01-cnf`):

1. `toCnf_eval (v) : ∀ b φ, Cnf.eval v (toCnf b φ) = (if b then eval v φ else !eval v φ)`
2. `taut_iff_cnf_unsat (φ) : Tautology φ ↔ (toCnf false φ).Unsat`

Try cold; §6 has hints.

## 6. Hints for the skeleton

**1 `toCnf_eval`.** *Nudge:* `intro b φ; induction φ generalizing b` (you need the IH at *both*
polarities). The `var`/`fls` cases are `cases b <;> simp [toCnf, …, Form.eval]`. For each connective,
`cases b`, then `simp` with `[toCnf, distribute_eval, cnf_eval_append, iha, ihc, Form.eval]`, and finish
the leftover Boolean identity with `cases Form.eval v a <;> cases Form.eval v c <;> rfl`. *More:* see the
shape in §3 — every branch is one `simp` plus a four-row `cases`.

**2 `taut_iff_cnf_unsat`.** *Nudge:* `constructor`; both directions are `intro …; rw [toCnf_eval]`
(or `at`) then `simp`. `Tautology φ` is `∀ v, eval v φ = true`; `Unsat` is `∀ v, Cnf.eval v _ = false`;
`toCnf_eval` at `b = false` says the latter's body is `!eval v φ`. *More:* forward —
`intro h v; rw [toCnf_eval]; simp [h v]`; backward — `intro h v; have hv := h v; rw [toCnf_eval] at hv;
simp at hv; exact hv`.

## 7. Exercises (optional, for fluency)

1. **The empty clause is unsatisfiable.** Prove `([[]] : Cnf).Unsat` (a clause set whose only clause is
   `□`). *Hint:* unfold and `simp`; the empty clause has nothing to satisfy.
2. **Use the bridge.** From `taut_imp_self` (Course 1: `Tautology (φ ⇒ φ)`), conclude
   `(toCnf false (Form.var 0 ⇒ Form.var 0)).Unsat`. *Hint:* it's one application of `taut_iff_cnf_unsat`.

## 8. Corrections to the optional exercises

### Exercise 1 — `□` is unsatisfiable

```lean
example : ([[]] : Cnf).Unsat := by
  intro v; simp [Cnf.eval, Clause.eval]
```

`Cnf.eval v [[]]` is "every clause is satisfied", and the only clause is `[]`, whose `Clause.eval` is
"some literal is true" over *no* literals — `false`. So the whole thing is `false` for every `v`: the
clause set is unsatisfiable. Deriving `□` from a clause set is therefore a certificate that the set has no
model — the entire point of resolution.

### Exercise 2 — refuting `∼(p ⇒ p)`

```lean
example : (toCnf false (Form.var 0 ⇒ Form.var 0)).Unsat :=
  (taut_iff_cnf_unsat _).mp (taut_imp_self _)
```

`taut_imp_self` says `p ⇒ p` is valid; the bridge converts that validity into unsatisfiability of the
clauses of its negation. Resolution will *find* that unsatisfiability by deriving `□` — which is exactly
slice 2.2.

## 9. Going further

- **Tseitin encoding.** Our `toCnf` is *equivalence*-preserving but can blow up in size (the `distribute`
  steps). Real solvers use the *Tseitin* transformation: introduce a fresh variable per subformula to get
  an *equisatisfiable* CNF of linear size. A worthwhile extension — the correctness statement weakens from
  "equivalent" to "equisatisfiable", which is all refutation needs.
- **Next: slice 2.2 — the resolution rule.** From clauses `C ∨ p` and `D ∨ ¬p`, derive `C ∨ D`; a
  *refutation* is a derivation of `□`. We define it as an inductive relation (echoing `Deriv` from 1.3)
  and build a refutation by hand.
